quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the vocabulary of activity-based costing and the four-product example.

questions.q: In activity-based costing, what is a cost driver?
options: The measure of an activity that causes its cost, such as the number of set-ups
The total fixed cost of the month
The selling price that covers all costs
The kilograms of material a product consumes
questions.explain: A cost driver is the activity measure that causes a pool of cost to be incurred; set-ups are driven by lots, not by kilograms. Kilograms are the volume base used by the conventional system, not an activity driver.

questions.q: In the lecture, conventional process costing spreads the whole Rs 440,000 of fixed cost on which basis?
questions.explain: The conventional sheet allocates all fixed cost in proportion to the kilograms each lot consumes (Rs 100 per kg on 4,400 kg). Spreading on lots is what ABC does for the set-up pool only.

questions.q: A set-up cost is incurred once per lot, whether the lot is 100 units or 1,000 units.
questions.explain: Every lot needs a Rs 50,000 set-up regardless of its size; that is exactly why spreading it on kilograms distorts the cost of small lots.

questions.q: Which two products does ABC reveal are being sold below their true cost at the conventional price?
questions.explain: A and C are the low-volume lots (100 units each). ABC shows losses of Rs 424.55 and Rs 273.64 per unit, while the high-volume B and D still earn a profit.

questions.q: Under the conventional costing sheet every one of the four products appears to earn the same 10 % margin.
questions.explain: Prices are set at cost plus 10 % from the conventional unit costs, so by construction each product shows 10 % — the sheet cannot reveal which products are really losing money.

questions.q: What name does the lecture give to the effect where large lots carry cost actually caused by small lots?
questions.explain: Volume distortion (cross-subsidy) is the key idea of the lecture: a volume base over-charges high-volume products and under-charges low-volume ones.

questions.q: Under ABC in the lecture, the Rs 240,000 of other fixed cost is spread on what?
questions.explain: Only the set-up is traced to lots; the remaining Rs 240,000 has no obvious driver, so it is still spread on kilograms (Rs 54.55 per kg). Spreading it on lots would be a different allocation.

questions.q: Which cost does ABC trace directly to the lot that caused it?
questions.explain: The set-up is an activity cost caused by each lot, so ABC charges Rs 50,000 to every lot. Material and labour are direct costs traced under both systems.

questions.q: Switching from conventional costing to ABC reduces the total fixed cost of the month.
questions.explain: ABC changes only how the Rs 440,000 is shared between products; the total cost of the month is the same under both systems.

questions.q: How is the total fixed cost of Rs 440,000 made up?
options: Rs 240,000 of set-ups plus Rs 200,000 of other fixed cost
Four set-ups × Rs 50,000 plus Rs 240,000 of other fixed cost
questions.explain: Four lots each need a Rs 50,000 set-up (Rs 200,000) and other fixed cost is Rs 240,000, giving Rs 440,000. The first option swaps the two figures.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How each line of the two costing systems is calculated and which way it moves when an input changes.

questions.q: Under conventional costing, the fixed cost allocated to a lot equals which expression?
options: Total fixed cost × (kg of the lot ÷ total kg of all products)
Total fixed cost ÷ number of lots
Set-up cost × units in the lot
Total fixed cost × (units of the lot ÷ total units)
questions.explain: The conventional sheet shares all fixed cost in proportion to kilograms: Rs 440,000 × 100 ÷ 4,400 = Rs 10,000 for product A. Dividing equally by lots is not volume-based costing.

questions.q: Total fixed cost is Rs 440,000 and all products together consume 4,400 kg. What is the conventional fixed-cost rate per kg?
questions.explain: Rs 440,000 ÷ 4,400 kg = Rs 100 per kg. Every kilogram carries the same share of fixed cost whichever lot it belongs to.

questions.q: Under ABC only the other fixed cost of Rs 240,000 is spread on 4,400 kg. What is the ABC rate per kg, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Rs 240,000 ÷ 4,400 kg = Rs 54.55 per kg. The other Rs 200,000 (four set-ups) is charged per lot instead.

questions.q: A lot's units are doubled while kg per unit stays the same. Under ABC, what happens to the set-up cost per unit?
questions.explain: Set-up is a fixed Rs 50,000 per lot, so set-up per unit = 50,000 ÷ units; doubling the units halves it. The material, labour and other-fixed parts per unit are unchanged.

questions.q: Under ABC, the set-up cost per unit is inversely proportional to the number of units in the lot.
questions.explain: Set-up per unit = Rs 50,000 ÷ units per lot, so 100 units give Rs 500 per unit and 1,000 units give Rs 50 per unit.

questions.q: Which component of the unit cost is identical under conventional costing and ABC?
options: Material plus direct labour per unit
questions.explain: Material and labour are Rs 100 per kg each under both systems, so they give the same Rs 200 per kg of material per unit; only the fixed-cost share changes.

questions.q: Set-up cost per lot rises from Rs 50,000 to Rs 60,000. Under conventional costing, how does the fixed cost charged to product D change?
options: It rises by the full Rs 40,000 increase
It rises by D's kilogram share of the Rs 40,000 increase
questions.explain: Total fixed cost rises by 4 × Rs 10,000 = Rs 40,000 and is spread on kg; D has 3,000 of 4,400 kg, so it absorbs Rs 27,273 of the increase. Under ABC it would absorb exactly Rs 10,000.

questions.q: Under ABC in the lecture, which part of product A's cost per lot still depends on the kilograms consumed by the other three products?
options: Other fixed cost allocated on kg
questions.explain: The other fixed cost rate is Rs 240,000 ÷ total kg, so if another product's kilograms change, A's share of the Rs 240,000 changes too. Set-up is a flat Rs 50,000 per lot.

questions.q: ABC gives a unit cost of Rs 754.55 for product A. What selling price would cost plus 10 % give, to the nearest paisa?
questions.explain: Rs 754.55 × 1.10 = Rs 830.01 — compared with the Rs 330 the conventional sheet quotes.

questions.q: How is the line 'profit per unit at the conventional price' calculated in the ABC sheet?
options: Conventional selling price − ABC total cost per unit
Conventional cost per unit − ABC cost per unit
Conventional selling price − conventional cost per unit
questions.explain: The lecture keeps the price marketing actually quotes (cost + 10 % from the conventional sheet) and deducts the ABC cost: 330 − 754.55 = (424.55) for A. The last option would always give the 10 % margin.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the four-product sheet and a few new lots with your calculator.

questions.q: Product A's lot has material plus labour of Rs 20,000 and allocated fixed cost of Rs 10,000, and its conventional cost per unit is Rs 300. How many units are in the lot?
Product C consumes 300 kg at Rs 200 per kg for material and labour, receives Rs 30,000 of allocated fixed cost and is made in a lot of 100 units. What is its conventional cost per unit?
questions.explain: Material and labour = 300 × 200 = Rs 60,000; plus Rs 30,000 fixed = Rs 90,000; ÷ 100 units = Rs 900 per unit.

questions.q: Under ABC product A carries material and labour of Rs 20,000, a set-up of Rs 50,000 and other fixed cost of Rs 5,455, for 100 units. What is the ABC cost per unit, to two decimals?
Product D: material and labour Rs 600,000, set-up Rs 50,000, other fixed cost Rs 163,636, lot of 1,000 units. What is the ABC cost per unit, to two decimals?
questions.explain: (600,000 + 50,000 + 163,636) ÷ 1,000 = 813,636 ÷ 1,000 = Rs 813.64 — lower than the conventional Rs 900 because D no longer subsidises the small lots.

questions.q: Product C sells at the conventional price of Rs 990 but its ABC cost is Rs 1,263.64 per unit. What is the profit per unit? (Give a loss as a negative number.)
questions.explain: 990 − 1,263.64 = −273.64, i.e. a loss of Rs 273.64 on every unit of C.

questions.q: A new product E is made in one lot of 200 units at 2 kg each. Material and labour cost Rs 200 per kg, the set-up is Rs 50,000 and other fixed cost is charged at Rs 54.55 per kg. What is its ABC cost per unit, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: Lot uses 400 kg: material and labour 400 × 200 = 80,000; other fixed 400 × 54.55 = 21,820; plus set-up 50,000 = Rs 151,820; ÷ 200 = Rs 759.10 ≈ Rs 759.

questions.q: Product A loses Rs 424.55 per unit at the conventional price and the lot is 100 units. What is the total loss on the lot, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 424.55 × 100 = Rs 42,455 lost on one small order that the conventional sheet shows as earning 10 %.

questions.q: Product B consumes 1,000 kg of the 4,400 kg total. What other fixed cost does ABC allocate to B's lot?
questions.explain: Rs 240,000 × 1,000 ÷ 4,400 = Rs 54,545. Rs 100,000 is what the conventional system allocates to B (Rs 440,000 × 1,000 ÷ 4,400).

questions.q: A small product sells at Rs 330. Its ABC cost excluding set-up is Rs 254.55 per unit (Rs 200 material and labour + Rs 54.55 other fixed) and each lot needs a Rs 50,000 set-up. How many units must a lot contain to break even? Round up to whole units.
questions.explain: Each unit contributes 330 − 254.55 = Rs 75.45 towards the set-up; 50,000 ÷ 75.45 = 662.7, so 663 units. Lots of 100 cannot recover their set-up at this price.

questions.q: Adding material and labour of Rs 880,000 to fixed cost of Rs 440,000, what is the total cost of all four lots, and does it differ between the two systems?
options: Rs 1,320,000 under conventional costing and Rs 1,120,000 under ABC
Rs 1,320,000 under ABC and Rs 1,520,000 under conventional costing
questions.explain: 880,000 + 440,000 = Rs 1,320,000 in both cases; ABC only redistributes the Rs 440,000 between lots, it never changes the total.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions a costing office or marketing team faces once the ABC picture is known.

questions.q: Marketing quotes 'cost plus 10 %' from the conventional sheet for a 100-unit order of product A. What is the most likely outcome?
options: A loss, because the Rs 50,000 set-up is far larger than the fixed cost the conventional sheet allocates
A profit higher than 10 %, because small lots use little material
questions.explain: The conventional sheet charges A only Rs 10,000 of fixed cost, but the lot really causes a Rs 50,000 set-up plus a share of other fixed cost; at Rs 330 the order loses about Rs 42,455.

questions.q: A customer offers to double the size of an order of product C from 100 to 200 units in a single lot. Under ABC, which statement is correct?
options: The set-up cost per unit halves, so C becomes much more profitable
Nothing changes because fixed cost is spread on kg
The set-up cost per lot doubles
questions.explain: The Rs 50,000 set-up is spread over 200 units instead of 100, cutting set-up per unit from Rs 500 to Rs 250. Material per unit is unchanged (3 kg per unit).

questions.q: A sensible response to the ABC findings is to quote a higher price, or a minimum order quantity, for small lots.
questions.explain: ABC shows each small lot must recover its own Rs 50,000 set-up; raising the price for small orders or setting a minimum lot size are both ways to do that.

questions.q: A mill's sales team argues that small orders 'keep the customer happy' and the large orders are very profitable anyway. What does the ABC sheet say about the large orders B and D?
options: They are more profitable than the conventional sheet shows, because they were carrying the small lots' set-ups
questions.explain: D's cost falls from Rs 900 to Rs 813.64 and B's from Rs 300 to Rs 304.55 (B rises slightly). The large lots had been subsidising A and C.

questions.q: A costing office wants to introduce ABC but has no record of how many lots each product is run in. What is the first thing it needs?
options: A record of activities (set-ups per lot) so each activity can be traced to the product that caused it
questions.explain: ABC depends on identifying activities and their drivers; without a count of set-ups per product the set-up pool cannot be traced and everything falls back on kilograms.

questions.q: Which of these cost items is best treated as an activity cost traced per lot rather than spread on kilograms?
options: The cost of changing dyes and cleaning the machine between orders
Electricity consumed in proportion to production
Cotton consumed per kg of yarn
Direct labour paid per kg processed
questions.explain: Changeover and cleaning cost is incurred once per order, so it is a set-up activity. The other three vary with volume and are correctly spread on kilograms.

questions.q: If every lot in the mill were the same size and used the same kg per unit, conventional costing and ABC would give the same unit costs.
questions.explain: Distortion arises only because lots differ in size; when all lots are identical, spreading set-ups on kg gives exactly Rs 50,000 per lot anyway.

questions.q: Product B (1,000 units, 1 kg each) rises from Rs 300.00 to Rs 304.55 per unit under ABC even though it is a high-volume product. Why?
options: Because its lot is high volume but small in kg, so the set-up per unit (Rs 50) is slightly more than the Rs 45.45 of fixed cost it no longer carries on kg
Because ABC always raises unit costs
questions.explain: B's fixed share changes from Rs 100 per unit to Rs 54.55 + Rs 50 set-up per unit = Rs 104.55, a rise of Rs 4.55. D (3 kg per unit) gains more because it drops Rs 300 of kg-based fixed cost per unit.

questions.q: The cheapest way for the mill to serve a customer who needs 100 units each of A and C every month is most likely to:
options: Run each as a separate 100-unit lot every month
Run a larger lot of each less often, so each set-up is spread over more units
questions.explain: Set-ups are the dominant cost of small lots; batching several months' demand into one lot spreads the Rs 50,000 over more units (holding stock has a cost too, but it is not in this lecture).

questions.q: A manager says ABC proves the set-up cost should be charged to customers as a separate 'set-up fee' of Rs 50,000 per order. Which objection is strongest?
options: Set-up cost is not a real cost
Customers with large orders would stop buying, because a flat fee hurts them most
A flat fee is reasonable for small lots, but the Rs 240,000 of other fixed cost still has to be recovered through the per-kg price
ABC does not allow set-up costs to be charged
questions.explain: Charging the set-up per order mirrors ABC exactly, but the other fixed cost and the margin must still be built into the per-kg price. A flat fee actually hurts small, not large, orders.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that combine the two sheets, two-step reasoning and the mistakes students most often make.

questions.q: Product D sells at Rs 990 and its ABC cost is Rs 813.64 per unit. What is its true margin as a percentage of price, to one decimal?
questions.explain: (990 − 813.64) ÷ 990 = 0.1781, i.e. 17.8 % — not the 10 % the conventional sheet shows (margin on price here, not on cost).

questions.q: A student computes ABC cost for product A as (20,000 + 50,000 + 10,000) ÷ 100 = Rs 800. What mistake has been made?
options: The other fixed cost should be A's share of Rs 240,000 (Rs 5,455), not the conventional allocation of all Rs 440,000 (Rs 10,000)
questions.explain: Rs 10,000 is A's kg share of the full Rs 440,000, which already includes the set-ups; adding a Rs 50,000 set-up on top double-counts. The correct other fixed share is 240,000 × 100 ÷ 4,400 = Rs 5,455.

questions.q: Suppose product C's lot were 300 units of 1 kg each instead of 100 units of 3 kg (still 300 kg). Material and labour Rs 60,000, set-up Rs 50,000, other fixed Rs 16,364. What is the ABC cost per unit, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Lot cost is unchanged at Rs 126,364 but spread over 300 units: 126,364 ÷ 300 = Rs 421.21. The same kilograms in more units gives a lower unit cost.

questions.q: Under conventional costing the fixed cost per unit of a small product (1 kg) is Rs 100 whether it is made in a lot of 100 or 1,000 units.
questions.explain: The conventional rate is Rs 100 per kg, so a 1 kg unit always carries Rs 100 of fixed cost; lot size is invisible to the system — which is the whole problem.

questions.q: Products A and C (100 units each) are dropped and the Rs 240,000 of other fixed cost is spread on the remaining 4,000 kg of B and D. Set-ups are still Rs 50,000 per lot. What is D's new ABC cost per unit (material and labour Rs 600,000, 3,000 kg, 1,000 units)?
questions.explain: Other fixed for D = 240,000 × 3,000 ÷ 4,000 = Rs 180,000; (600,000 + 50,000 + 180,000) ÷ 1,000 = Rs 830. Dropping products does not remove the other fixed cost, so D's cost rises from Rs 813.64.

questions.q: After dropping A and C, D's ABC unit cost rises from Rs 813.64 to Rs 830. What lesson follows?
options: ABC was wrong about A and C
Fixed cost that does not disappear when a product is dropped is simply re-spread on the survivors, so dropping loss-makers is not automatically the answer
Set-up cost rises when products are dropped
questions.explain: The Rs 240,000 is fixed; removing A and C removes only their set-ups (truly avoidable) and leaves the rest to be carried by B and D. Repricing or batching the small lots may be better than dropping them.

questions.q: Conventional profit on product A's lot of 100 units at Rs 330 with unit cost Rs 300 is Rs 3,000. The ABC loss on the same lot is Rs 42,455. By how much does the conventional sheet overstate A's lot profit?
questions.explain: From +3,000 to −42,455 is a swing of Rs 45,455. The same amount is spread as hidden extra cost over B, C and D in the conventional sheet.

questions.q: Which product's cost per unit changes the most between the two systems?
questions.explain: A rises by Rs 454.55 per unit (151 %); C rises by Rs 363.64 (40 %). Both are small lots of 100 units, but A's set-up is spread over the fewest kilograms, so the distortion is largest.

questions.q: A mill halves its set-up cost to Rs 25,000 per lot by better planning. Which product's ABC unit cost falls the most in rupees?
options: A and C fall by Rs 250 each
B and D fall by Rs 25 each
questions.explain: Saving Rs 25,000 per lot is Rs 250 per unit on a 100-unit lot (A and C) but only Rs 25 per unit on a 1,000-unit lot (B and D). Set-up reductions help small lots most.

questions.q: In the ABC sheet, the sum of 'set-up cost per lot' and 'other fixed cost per lot' across the four products equals:
questions.explain: 4 × 50,000 = 200,000 plus 5,455 + 54,545 + 16,364 + 163,636 = 240,000 gives Rs 440,000 — the same total the conventional sheet allocates. Rs 880,000 is material and labour.
